discussion_feedback: The discussion clearly passes and fits Tier 2 overall. The student revisits the hypothesis, states a main conclusion, interprets the main findings at the construct level, and compares the results to prior research from the introduction. The unexpected waitlist increase is explicitly discussed and several possible explanations are proposed, which is an important strength. Limitations and future research directions are present and are somewhat study-specific, including sample size, use of one therapist, and restricted treatment format. The broader practical implication of self-led VRET accessibility is also argued. It falls short of Tier 3 because the reasoning is not consistently complete and critical throughout: the theoretical framework is revisited, but only somewhat briefly and not deeply evaluated in terms of whether it should be refined; alternative explanations are raised but not systematically weighed; and some implications are a bit stronger than the data warrant. The discussion is solidly average-to-above-average for this level, but not fully in the 'good' tier.
lang_style_feedback: The paper is generally understandable and scientifically written, so it clearly passes Tier 2. Sections are recognizable, most paragraphs have a discernible focus, and grammar/spelling errors are present but not overwhelming. However, the language is not polished enough for Tier 3. There are multiple awkward phrasings, some redundancy, several APA and formatting inconsistencies, and a few citation/reference issues (for example inconsistent capitalization, errors in author formatting, year mismatch in-text versus references for Bouchard, and irregular reference formatting). Some sentences are longer or clumsier than needed, and transitions are sometimes mechanical rather than smooth. Overall, the writing is adequate and readable, but not near-faultless.

intro_feedback:
The introduction has a clear topic, establishes societal relevance well enough, and ends with a clear aim and hypothesis. The student discusses why accessible treatment for SAD matters and connects this reasonably to online and self-led VR treatment. The research question is relevant and grounded in prior work. The paper also includes the required core SAD-VR studies and an additional article that fits the self-led focus. A strength is that the student does not only summarize findings, but often explains why each study matters for the current design. The theoretical ideas about exposure, self-efficacy, and therapist guidance are also linked to the hypotheses.

The main limitation is coherence and precision of the argument. The introduction is often more study-by-study than fully synthesized, and some transitions are weak or overstated. Parts of the theoretical framework are not very rigorous: Vygotsky's zone of proximal development is applied somewhat loosely to therapist-led treatment, and the comparison between interaction theory and self-efficacy theory is not fully developed as a strong integrated framework. Some critiques of prior studies are also not always convincing or fully accurate. There are several citation inconsistencies (e.g., Anderson year in text vs reference list), and some claims rely on less suitable sources such as websites where stronger empirical evidence would have helped. Still, for this level the line of reasoning is overall coherent, relevant, and sufficiently convincing, which places the section in the good range rather than merely adequate.
methods_feedback:
The method is coherent with the stated research question and hypotheses, and the basic structure with Participants, Materials, and Procedure is present. The design can be understood: three conditions, pre-post assessment, and LSAS as the main outcome. Inclusion and exclusion criteria are given, recruitment is described, and the treatment conditions are differentiated in a way that generally fits the study aims.

However, the section is only somewhat comprehensively described and misses several elements that the writing guide expects. Participant information is incomplete: there is no mean age and standard deviation in the Participants subsection, no exact gender counts there, no compensation or reward, and no explanation of how diagnosis and the 'criteria for the social phobia scale' were established. Allocation is said to be random, but the procedure for randomization is not described. The Materials section is also underdeveloped in places: the LSAS description is partly useful, but includes an incorrect statement that the questionnaire itself is analyzed through multiple regression, which confuses measurement with analysis. Important psychometric or cut-off information is mostly absent. For the interventions, there is some description of the VR scenarios, but standardization across therapist-led and self-led conditions is not sufficiently detailed, and the distinction between what is fixed and what is tailored is only partly clear. In the Procedure section, the chronology is understandable, but timing and implementation details are still fairly sparse. Overall, the method is nearly complete and mostly correct, but not complete and correct enough for a higher score.
results_feedback:
The results section follows the expected overall structure at a basic level: it states the analysis, gives a demographics table, reports assumption checks, reports main effects and an interaction, and summarizes post-hoc comparisons in understandable language. The findings are relevant to the design and hypotheses, and the interpretation of the interaction is clear enough.

That said, the section has several important reporting problems that keep it at the lower end of passing. Most notably, Table 2 is announced but the actual means and standard deviations for the main outcome are missing. According to the course expectations and sample results, descriptive statistics for the outcome per condition and time point are essential. The ANOVA degrees of freedom also appear incorrect or at least inconsistent with the design: with three conditions and two time points, the reported dfs of F(1, 99) for both main effects and the interaction do not fit well. There is also a likely sample-size inconsistency, since 99 participants would usually imply error dfs around 96 or similar depending on the effect, not 99 throughout. Reporting format is uneven ('p = <.001', inconsistent spacing, incomplete punctuation). The figure is referenced but not actually shown in the submitted text. Because the core analytic story is still understandable and mostly aligned with the stated design, this section passes, but only narrowly.
discussion_feedback:
The discussion clearly restates the aim, answers the research question, and indicates which hypotheses were supported and not supported. The student also does more than merely repeat the results: they compare the findings with prior research, explain the unexpected superiority of self-led VR relative to therapist-led VR, and revisit the theoretical ideas introduced earlier. The section includes several concrete limitations and future directions that are reasonably specific to the study rather than entirely generic. The broader implications for accessibility and waitlists are also logically connected to the findings.

The main weaknesses are in depth and precision of reasoning. Some interpretations are stronger than the data justify, especially when moving from a pre-post study with no follow-up to broader claims about implementation and societal benefits. The discussion does acknowledge this to some extent, but the final paragraph becomes somewhat promotional. The integration with prior literature is decent but not fully balanced: some explanations are speculative and not always well substantiated. The theoretical reflection is present, yet it remains somewhat simplistic, treating the findings as support for self-efficacy and not for interaction theory without sufficiently considering overlap, alternative mechanisms, or the fact that neither mechanism was directly measured. Still, the section is relevant, mostly coherent, and shows good engagement with the findings and limitations, which supports a solid adequate-to-good grade.
lang_style_feedback:
The paper is generally readable and the overall structure is clear. Most sections and paragraphs have an identifiable focus, and the scientific tone is mostly appropriate for this level. The reader can usually follow the argument from introduction through discussion.

There are, however, quite a few language and APA issues. Grammar and phrasing are regularly awkward ('people their', 'an virtual environment', 'would continue treatment later'), punctuation is inconsistent, and several sentences are overly long or insufficiently edited. There are also citation and reference inconsistencies, including year mismatches, punctuation problems, and formatting errors. Statistical notation is not consistently APA-style. Some wording is vague or repetitive, and a few claims are imprecise. These issues do not seriously block understanding, but they are frequent enough to keep the score around average rather than good.

intro_feedback: The introduction presents a clear and relevant topic, establishes societal relevance early, and works toward a specific research question comparing self-led VRET, therapist-led VRET, and waitlist for SAD. The student includes a theoretical rationale using exposure principles, self-efficacy, and interaction theory, and discusses several relevant empirical studies, including the required core VRET literature and an additional study fitting the specific focus. The overall line of reasoning is coherent enough for this level and the hypothesis is clearly stated. Stronger aspects are the attempt to connect accessibility, waitlists, and self-led interventions to the proposed study, and the effort to explain why prior studies do not fully answer the current question. However, the argumentation is only somewhat convincing rather than fully convincing. Much of the literature review remains study-by-study rather than well synthesized, some critique of earlier studies is overstated or not always logically tied to the present design, and there are factual/citation inconsistencies (e.g., Anderson year mismatch, Bandura year mismatch, use of broad or nonacademic sources for key claims). The theoretical framework is present but somewhat loosely integrated, and the final justification for why self-led and therapist-led should work equally well is not argued very tightly. Overall this fits between adequate and good, leaning adequate-to-good.
methods_feedback: The method section describes a coherent design that matches the stated research question: three conditions with pre- and post-measurement. Participants, materials, and procedure are all present, and the basic intervention differences between SVRET, TVRET, and waitlist are understandable. The use of the LSAS is appropriate for SAD, and the procedure gives a reasonable overview of the 10-week treatment format. These elements support a passing grade. At the same time, important required details are missing or insufficiently specified. Participant selection is vague: 'chosen randomly' is unclear, inclusion criteria are incomplete, and no justification is given for the criteria. Key sample details are incomplete because there is no mean age with SD in the Participants section, and no compensation/reward information is reported. Allocation is mentioned as random, but the randomization procedure is not explained. The Materials section lacks some expected operational detail for the LSAS, such as clearer scoring description and more precise reporting of the instrument format; it also includes analysis information ('multiple regression') that does not belong there and is inconsistent with the Results. Replicability is only moderate because several procedural details remain underspecified, such as how therapists interacted during online sessions, whether assessments were self-report online, and how adherence in the self-led condition was monitored. Therefore, the methods are coherent and nearly complete, but not fully complete or fully correct.
results_feedback: The student reports the intended analysis in a structure resembling the sample results section: descriptive demographics, assumption checks, omnibus mixed ANOVA, and post-hoc comparisons. The narrative of the findings is understandable and linked to the design. However, the section is only just adequate because there are several important completeness and correctness issues. Most notably, Table 2 is announced but the actual means and standard deviations for the main outcome across time and condition are missing, and Figure 1 is referenced but not actually presented in the text provided. This is a major omission because the sample results explicitly expect descriptive outcome statistics. There are also statistical inconsistencies: with three conditions and two time points, the reported ANOVA degrees of freedom for condition and interaction appear incorrect, suggesting misunderstanding or incorrect reporting. Some p-value formatting is also inaccurate (e.g., 'p = <.001'). Assumption checks are brief and acceptable for level, but not especially precise. Because the reporting is somewhat coherent but incomplete and partly incorrect in relation to the stated design, this section falls at the lower bound of passing.
discussion_feedback: The discussion clearly restates the aim, answers the research question, and distinguishes between supported and unsupported hypotheses. The student interprets the main pattern of findings, connects them back to prior literature, and explicitly discusses the unexpected result that self-led VRET outperformed therapist-led VRET. This is a strength, because the discussion does not ignore the surprising finding. The student also links the findings back to the theoretical framework, especially self-efficacy and interaction theory, and includes multiple study-specific limitations and concrete future research suggestions. The broader implications for accessibility and waitlists are also appropriately tied back to the introduction. These features support a solid grade. The section is not stronger because some interpretations are still somewhat speculative and not always sufficiently constrained by the data. For example, the discussion tends to infer underlying mechanisms such as self-efficacy without having measured them, and some literature integration remains more confirmatory than analytical. There are also some overstatements in the conclusion and practical implications given the limited design and absence of follow-up. Still, for a second-year first paper, the reasoning is mostly correct, coherent, and relevant, with meaningful critical reflection.
lang_style_feedback: The paper is generally readable and the scientific intent is clear throughout. The overall structure follows the expected paper format, and most sections and paragraphs have an identifiable topic. The reader can follow the main argument, and citation use is mostly functional. However, language and style are only at a developing-to-adequate level. There are frequent grammar and phrasing problems ('people their,' article/preposition errors, punctuation problems, spacing issues), several awkward or informal formulations, and multiple APA inconsistencies in both citations and references. There are also factual/sloppy presentation issues such as the impossible date ('December 6486th, 2025'), inconsistent study years, inconsistent naming, and some redundancy. Some paragraphs are overly long and would benefit from clearer PEEL structure and sharper transitions. Because these issues do not completely impede understanding but are too frequent for a higher score, the language/style grade is passing but modest.

intro_feedback: The introduction contains a clear societal starting point, explains why SAD matters, and builds toward a relevant research question comparing self-led VRET, therapist-led VRET, and waitlist. The paper also includes a theoretical attempt using self-efficacy and interaction theory, and it discusses the required core studies plus an additional study relevant to self-led VR. This shows responsible use of sources and a generally coherent line toward the hypothesis. However, the argumentation is only somewhat convincing rather than strong. The literature review is often study-by-study instead of fully synthesized, some critiques of previous studies are simplistic or not always well justified, and there are several factual/citation inaccuracies (e.g., mismatches in years, Bandura cited differently, some overstatements about prior findings). The final hypothesis is clear, but the reasoning for expecting equal effects of SVRET and TVRET is less convincing than the reasoning that both should outperform waitlist. Overall this fits an adequate-to-good introduction, closer to adequate/good boundary.
methods_feedback: The method is coherent and matches the stated research question and hypotheses. The key subsections are present, and the overall design can be understood: three conditions, pre-post assessment, 10-week intervention, and LSAS as outcome measure. Participants are described with sample size, age range, gender proportions, recruitment route, and exclusion criteria. Materials and procedure also give a usable overview of the VR scenarios and how the conditions differ. However, important details are missing or imprecise for replication. The paper does not report mean age and SD in the Participants section as requested, compensation is absent, random allocation is mentioned but not explained, and the phrase that participants were 'chosen randomly' after registration is unclear. The Materials section includes some procedural content, and the analysis plan is incorrectly described there as 'multiple regression' while the Results use mixed ANOVA. Description of the LSAS is partly adequate but not fully precise in psychometric/administration terms. So the method is mostly complete and mostly correct, but not fully complete or fully clear.
results_feedback: The Results section follows the expected general structure: it names the analysis, reports assumption checks, includes a demographics table, gives inferential results, and describes post-hoc comparisons in understandable language. discussion_feedback: The discussion clearly restates the aim, answers the research question, and distinguishes between supported and unsupported parts of the hypothesis. lang_style_feedback: The paper is generally readable and the overall structure is clear, with recognizable sections and a mostly scientific tone. intro_feedback: The introduction presents a clear and relevant research question and gives a coherent hourglass structure from societal relevance to theory, prior research, and hypotheses. Societal relevance is established well for adolescents specifically, and the paper explains why a comparison between VRET and IVET matters for this population. The theoretical framework is present and used to motivate exposure-based treatment, although it is somewhat simplified and at times not fully precise. The line of reasoning toward the prediction that VRET should outperform IVET in adolescents is generally understandable, but the argument is not fully convincing because it leans on assumptions about adolescents’ familiarity/comfort with technology more than on strong direct evidence. The required core studies are discussed and linked to the current design, and the student includes an additional adolescent-focused article appropriately. The literature review goes beyond pure summary, but synthesis across studies could still be stronger and some interpretations are a bit overstated. The final aim, hypotheses, and design are clearly stated. Overall, this is a good, above-average introduction with a visible scientific storyline, though not maximally tight or fully convincing throughout.
methods_feedback: The method is coherent and clearly related to the stated research question and hypotheses. The basic structure with Participants, Materials, and Procedure is appropriate, and the student includes important elements such as recruitment, diagnosis, exclusion criteria, random assignment, treatment conditions, and the main dependent measure. The intervention descriptions are reasonably detailed for this level, especially for VRET, and the procedure is chronological and mostly understandable. However, the section is not fully complete according to the writing guide. Key participant details such as mean age, standard deviation, and gender composition are not reported in Participants but only later in Results. Inclusion criteria are implied but not explicitly justified. The IVET condition is described less precisely than the VRET condition, making comparability between conditions somewhat less clear. Overall, the methods are complete enough and mostly correct, but some expected details are missing or unevenly distributed, so this fits between adequate and good.
results_feedback: The results section is mostly correct, complete, and easy to follow for this student level. It follows the expected sample structure reasonably well: there is a demographics table, a table with means and standard deviations for the main outcome, reporting of the mixed ANOVA, an assumption check, and post-hoc comparisons. The operational level reporting is clear, and the interaction is interpreted appropriately. The section also appropriately notes that both treatment groups outperformed waitlist at post-test while VRET did not significantly outperform IVET. This is the core pattern that needed to be conveyed. There are some weaknesses: assumption reporting is somewhat limited, the Central Limit Theorem justification is a bit mechanically applied, and the statement that N is bigger than 30 is crude when group sizes are 30. The results text also briefly comments that findings matched or contradicted hypotheses, which slightly shifts toward discussion. In addition, the significance of the waitlist decrease is noteworthy and could have been framed more carefully in relation to the interaction pattern. Still, compared with the sample expectations for this course, the section is solid and above average.
discussion_feedback: The discussion is the strongest section. It begins with a clear main conclusion that answers the research question directly and distinguishes supported from unsupported hypotheses. The student then interprets the main findings in relation to prior literature and the proposed theoretical framework, rather than merely repeating the results. Importantly, the unexpected finding that VRET did not outperform IVET is not ignored; instead, the student offers a substantive interpretation involving cognitive avoidance and the possible added value of CBT. That reasoning is thoughtful and shows good scientific engagement, even if some parts remain speculative. The discussion also includes theory implications, limitations that are fairly study-specific rather than purely generic, and concrete future research suggestions that follow from those limitations. Broader implications for adolescent treatment engagement are also brought back at the end. Some claims are somewhat stronger than the data warrant, particularly where mechanisms are inferred without direct measurement, and the significant symptom decrease in the waitlist condition could have been interrogated more critically because it is a striking finding. Even so, the discussion is coherent, relevant, and convincingly argued for this course level, making it above average.
lang_style_feedback: The paper is generally clearly written and organized, with a readable scientific style and mostly coherent paragraph structure. The overall flow is easy to follow, especially in the introduction and discussion, and citations are generally used responsibly. There are some language issues, awkward phrasings, and sentence-level imprecision throughout the paper. A few terminology and factual slips are present, such as inconsistent naming, minor grammatical problems, and some APA/reference inconsistencies. There is also occasional redundancy and some sentences are longer or less polished than ideal. However, these issues do not substantially impede understanding. For this level, the writing is clearly above insufficient and around good readability, but not near-faultless.

intro_feedback: The introduction is clearly above average for this course level. It opens with a relevant societal problem focused on adolescents, explains why this population matters, and builds toward a clear research question and hypotheses. The theoretical framework is present and meaningfully connected to the treatments: conditioning mechanisms, avoidance, and how exposure might work are used to justify why VRET and IVET should reduce symptoms. The literature review includes the required core studies (Anderson et al., Kampmann et al., Bouchard et al.) plus an additional adolescent-focused study, and these are generally used as building blocks rather than listed entirely separately. The final paragraph gives a clear aim, design, and hypotheses. Strong points are the population-specific relevance, logical transition from theory to treatment rationale, and the attempt to explain why adolescents might especially benefit from VRET. The main limitation preventing a higher grade is that the line of reasoning is not always equally tight: some claims are somewhat speculative (e.g., adolescents’ familiarity with VR leading to superior effectiveness), and the review sometimes slips into study-by-study summary rather than full synthesis. There are also a few small conceptual inaccuracies or oversimplifications in the explanation of conditioning and treatment mechanisms. Still, overall the introduction is coherent, relevant, and convincingly argued for this level.
methods_feedback: The methods section is solid and coherent, and the design clearly matches the stated research question and hypotheses. Participants, exclusion criteria, random assignment, treatment conditions, dependent measure, and overall procedure are all described. The intervention descriptions are reasonably detailed for a second-year paper, especially for VRET, and the procedure gives a clear chronological overview from screening to post-treatment assessment. The LSAS-CA is also described with developer, item structure, scale, scoring range, and cut-off, which aligns well with the writing guide. The main reasons the grade is not higher are missing details that matter for completeness and replicability. Inclusion criteria are present, but recruitment and diagnostic assessment could be described more precisely. The allocation procedure is mentioned, but there is limited detail on who conducted randomization or whether allocation concealment occurred. IVET is described more briefly than VRET, making the balance between conditions less clear. Overall, the section is complete enough and mostly correct, but not fully comprehensive.
results_feedback: The results section is clearly structured and closely follows the expected sample format, which is a strength. It includes a demographics table, descriptive statistics for the main outcome, assumption checks, the main mixed ANOVA, and Holm-corrected post-hoc comparisons. The reporting is understandable and appropriately tied to the design. The interpretation of the interaction is clear, and the reader can follow which hypotheses were supported and which were not. This is around the baseline of a good student results section for this assignment. The section is not higher because there are some weaknesses in statistical reporting and precision. The normality reasoning is somewhat simplistic, and the statement that N = 90 justifies CLT is acceptable at this level but not very nuanced; also, group sizes are 30, so this could have been phrased more carefully. Some APA/statistical formatting is inconsistent (spacing, p-value formatting, punctuation). The results occasionally become slightly interpretive rather than staying purely descriptive, for example explicitly referring to expectations of the hypotheses. The figure itself is referenced but not actually shown in the provided text. Still, the analyses are mostly correct, complete, coherent, and relevant to the stated design.
discussion_feedback: The discussion is one of the stronger sections. It begins with a clear main conclusion that answers the research question and states which hypotheses were supported and not supported. It then relates the findings to previous literature and theory in a generally coherent way. The student does more than restate results: they try to explain why VRET was not superior to IVET, using the idea of cognitive avoidance and the possible added value of CBT. This is a good example of interpretation grounded in prior theory and research rather than simply repeating outcomes. The section also includes relevant limitations that are specific to the design, such as semi-structured avatar dialogues and therapeutic alliance differences between conditions, and these are used to motivate sensible future research directions. Broader implications are present and return to the issue of making treatment attractive for adolescents. In addition, the discussion could engage more critically with the surprising improvement in the waitlist group, because that is an important pattern in the results and deserves deeper consideration. Despite that, the reasoning is coherent, relevant, and above average for this course level.

The sections are easy to follow, paragraphing is mostly logical, and the scientific tone is appropriate for the assignment. Sentences are usually understandable and the argument is communicated clearly. APA use is mostly responsible, with in-text citations and a substantial reference list. methods_feedback: The Methods section is clearly present and broadly coherent with the stated RQ and hypotheses. intro_feedback: De introductie bevat een duidelijke en grotendeels coherente redenering van maatschappelijke relevantie naar onderzoeksvraag en hypothesen. De maatschappelijke relevantie van SAS bij adolescenten wordt vroeg benoemd, kernbegrippen worden uitgelegd, en de keuze voor VRET versus IVET versus wachtlijst wordt logisch opgebouwd. Ook is er zichtbaar geprobeerd theorie te gebruiken, vooral via het cognitief-gedragsmatige model van sociale angst en via argumenten over adolescent-specifieke kenmerken zoals schaamte en faalangst. De hypothesen zijn expliciet geformuleerd en sluiten aan op het voorgaande. Sterk is ook dat de student niet alleen beschrijft dat VRET mogelijk werkt, maar probeert te onderbouwen waarom dit bij adolescenten anders zou kunnen uitpakken dan bij volwassenen. Tegelijk zijn er enkele beperkingen die een hogere beoordeling verhinderen. De literatuur is niet altijd optimaal geselecteerd of correct gekoppeld aan de opdracht: de verplichte kernstudies worden niet allemaal op de bedoelde manier besproken, en Kampmann et al. (2016) lijkt hier onjuist gebruikt te worden als empirische RCT in plaats van meta-analyse. Daarnaast is de literatuurbespreking soms nog wat samenvattend in plaats van echt synthetiserend, en de overgang van theorie naar exacte onderzoeksopzet had compacter en scherper gekund. Ook zitten er enkele kleine onnauwkeurigheden in de argumentatie en referentie-inzet. Al met al is de introductie duidelijk boven gemiddeld: coherent, relevant en overtuigend, maar nog niet sterk genoeg geïntegreerd voor een 8 of hoger.
methods_feedback: De methode is in de kern coherent en sluit goed aan op de onderzoeksvraag en hypothesen. De keuze voor drie condities past logisch bij het doel om zowel werkzaamheid vast te stellen als VRET met IVET te vergelijken. De deelnemerssectie bevat relevante basisinformatie zoals leeftijd, spreiding, genderverdeling, inclusie- en exclusiecriteria en random toewijzing. Ook de procedure is voldoende begrijpelijk en chronologisch beschreven, met een duidelijke schets van wat er in elke conditie gebeurt. Dat de student motiveert waarom IVET deels zelfstandig werd uitgevoerd, laat zien dat er is nagedacht over ontwerpkeuzes. Er zijn echter ook duidelijke onvolkomenheden. De sectie is minder volledig dan de writing guide vraagt: informatie over beloning/compensatie ontbreekt, groepsgrootten per conditie worden niet expliciet gegeven, en er is geen aparte analysesectie. De beschrijving van materialen is bovendien erg summier voor de interventies: van VRET en IVET wordt onvoldoende precies beschreven welke scenario's of manipulaties gebruikt worden, wat exact gestandaardiseerd is tussen condities, en hoe de protocollen concreet zijn toegepast. Voor de LSAS-CA is de beschrijving redelijk volledig, maar bijvoorbeeld betrouwbaarheid of wijze van afname ontbreekt. Verder roept de IVET-procedure methodologische vragen op doordat de blootstelling 'zelfstandig' buiten het lab gebeurt maar toch binnen de sessie en met terugkoppeling; dit is begrijpelijk beschreven, maar maakt de operationalisatie minder strak. Daarom is dit een degelijke, adequate methode voor dit niveau, maar niet volledig of precies genoeg voor een hogere score.
results_feedback: De resultaten zijn overwegend relevant voor het design en grotendeels begrijpelijk gerapporteerd, maar blijven wat achter bij het niveau van de sample results en bevatten meerdere onnauwkeurigheden. Positief is dat de student een passende mixed ANOVA gebruikt voor het 3 x 2 design, een tabel met gemiddelden en standaarddeviaties opneemt, en vervolgens post-hocvergelijkingen bespreekt. De hoofdconclusie uit de analyse is duidelijk weergegeven: beide actieve behandelingen verbeteren meer dan wachtlijst, en VRET lijkt sterker dan IVET. Dat sluit goed aan op de onderzoeksvraag. Toch zijn er verschillende tekortkomingen die de score drukken. De rapportage van assumpties is erg summier en deels onjuist geformuleerd (bijvoorbeeld 'Shaprio-Wilk-assumptie' en 'homogeniteit van variaties'), zonder nadere uitwerking zoals in het voorbeeld. De demografische tabel ontbreekt volledig, terwijl die volgens de richtlijnen wel verwacht wordt. De tabel met uitkomsten is nuttig maar beperkt; er is geen volledige descriptieve rapportage per conditie in combinatie met steekproefinformatie. Ook is de formulering soms slordig of inconsistent, bijvoorbeeld 'effectscore' in de figuur, de zin met 'als.', en het gebruik van t-waarden/post-hocrapportage zonder voldoende toelichting op welke vergelijkingen precies zijn uitgevoerd. Daarnaast wordt in de interpretatie van de resultaten al enigszins vooruitgelopen op de discussie ('in lijn met eerder onderzoek'). Voor dit niveau is de sectie nog voldoende en grotendeels correct, maar niet compleet en niet strak genoeg uitgewerkt om boven gemiddeld hoog te scoren.
discussion_feedback: De discussie is een sterk onderdeel van het paper. De student begint met een heldere hoofdconclusie waarin doel, onderzoeksvraag en hypothesen expliciet worden teruggepakt. Vervolgens worden de bevindingen logisch besproken in relatie tot eerdere literatuur, waarbij goed onderscheid wordt gemaakt tussen verwachte en onverwachte uitkomsten. Vooral sterk is dat het opvallende resultaat — VRET effectiever dan IVET — niet wordt genegeerd maar juist centraal wordt geïnterpreteerd. De student biedt meerdere plausibele verklaringen, waaronder ervaren controle, aansluiting bij adolescent-specifieke kenmerken en verschillen in therapeutische begeleiding. Ook wordt kritisch gereflecteerd op het feit dat deze verklaringen niet direct getest zijn, wat de discussie wetenschappelijk zorgvuldiger maakt. Daarnaast benoemt de student een belangrijke mogelijke confound, namelijk het verschil in begeleiding tussen condities, en werkt dit uit tot concreet vervolgonderzoek met een verbeterd design. Dat is een duidelijk pluspunt. Er zijn wel enkele beperkingen. De discussie is soms aan de lange kant en bevat herhaling van vergelijkbare verklaringen. Sommige interpretaties zijn speculatief en steunen op bredere aannames die niet direct uit de data volgen. Verder had de koppeling aan het theoretisch kader nog explicieter gekund: de theorie uit de introductie wordt wel gebruikt, maar niet helemaal systematisch geëvalueerd in termen van welke onderdelen ondersteund of juist niet getest zijn. Ook had een iets scherpere reflectie op de sterkte van de conclusies passend geweest. Desondanks is dit een overtuigende en bovengemiddelde discussie, met relevante interpretatie, kritische reflectie en praktische implicaties.
lang_style_feedback: De tekst is over het algemeen goed leesbaar, logisch opgebouwd en passend wetenschappelijk van toon voor dit niveau. Ook zijn er APA-onnauwkeurigheden en inconsistenties in bronvermelding en referenties, waaronder jaartallen die niet overal overeenkomen met de tekst, inconsistent hoofdlettergebruik, en enkele referenties die niet netjes zijn uitgewerkt. intro_feedback: De introductie is inhoudelijk relevant en bouwt redelijk duidelijk toe naar de onderzoeksvraag: maatschappelijke relevantie wordt vroeg genoemd, kernbegrippen worden uitgelegd, en er wordt uiteindelijk een concrete verwachting geformuleerd over VRET, IVET en de wachtlijstconditie. Sterk is dat de tekst probeert theorie (vermijding, zelfgerichte aandacht, vicieuze cirkel) te koppelen aan de behandelvormen en aan adolescentie-specifieke kenmerken. Een belangrijk minpunt is dat de verplichte kernstudies uit de cursus niet helemaal correct en strategisch worden gebruikt: Anderson et al. (2013) ontbreekt in de lopende tekst, Kampmann et al. wordt feitelijk onjuist weergegeven (2015 RCT wordt besproken, terwijl 2016 in de richtlijnen de bedoelde SAD-studie is), en de opbouw blijft deels beschrijvend in plaats van echt synthetisch. Ook zitten er enkele logische sprongen in de redenering van PSA naar bredere SAS, en sommige claims over adolescenten en VRET worden wat speculatief gebracht. Desondanks is de RQ/hypothese duidelijk en wetenschappelijk relevant, en de lijn van redeneren is overwegend coherent voor dit niveau.
methods_feedback: De methode is in de kern coherent en passend bij de onderzoeksvraag: er is een duidelijk experimenteel design met drie condities, relevante inclusie- en exclusiecriteria, en een passende afhankelijke maat. Positief is ook dat de steekproef basisdemografie bevat (leeftijd, SD, genderverdeling) en dat random toewijzing wordt genoemd. De beschrijving van de LSAS-CA is behoorlijk volledig, met items, schaal, scorebereik en interpretatie. Toch zijn er meerdere onvolledigheden die de reproduceerbaarheid beperken. De beschrijving van de interventies is te summier: voor VRET ontbreekt grotendeels welke virtuele sociale situaties precies zijn gebruikt, hoe moeilijkheid werd opgebouwd, en wat precies gestandaardiseerd was tussen condities. Voor IVET blijft onduidelijk welke opdrachten concreet werden uitgevoerd. Verder ontbreken beloning/compensatie, de precieze allocatieprocedure, en belangrijke details over wie de LSAS-CA afnam en hoe diagnose van SAS werd vastgesteld. Ook is er sectievermenging: onderdelen van materiaal en procedure lopen wat door elkaar. De methode is dus voldoende en grotendeels correct, maar niet echt volledig uitgewerkt.
results_feedback: De resultatensectie rapporteert de hoofdanalyse in een herkenbare en grotendeels passende vorm voor dit vak: er is een descriptieve tabel met pre- en postgemiddelden per conditie, een mixed ANOVA, en post-hocvergelijkingen. De tekst maakt ook duidelijk welk patroon gevonden is en koppelt dat aan de hypothesen. Dat is positief. Tegelijk zijn er meerdere tekortkomingen ten opzichte van de voorbeeldstructuur en de rubric. Er ontbreekt een demografische tabel, terwijl die expliciet verwacht wordt. De assumptierapportage is slordig en deels onjuist geformuleerd: er wordt gesproken over de 'Shaprio-Wilk-assumptie voor normaliteit en homogeniteit van variaties', terwijl homogeniteit niet met Shapiro-Wilk wordt getest. Ook is de reporting van post-hoc testen niet geheel consistent of transparant; bijvoorbeeld de vrijheidsgraden en gekozen toetsen worden niet goed uitgelegd, en de zin 'als.' wijst op een redactionele fout. Daarnaast wordt Figuur 1 wel genoemd maar inhoudelijk niet echt geïntegreerd en in de aangeleverde tekst niet zichtbaar uitgewerkt. De analyses zijn dus meestal relevant en begrijpelijk, maar de sectie is net niet volledig en statistisch wat slordig.
discussion_feedback: De discussie is het sterkste onderdeel van het paper. De eerste alinea geeft helder de onderzoeksvraag, de kernbevindingen en de status van de hypothesen weer. Daarna wordt het onverwachte resultaat — dat VRET effectiever was dan IVET — niet genegeerd maar juist actief geïnterpreteerd, wat volgens de rubric zwaar meeweegt. Sterk is ook dat de student meerdere mogelijke verklaringen bespreekt, waaronder adolescent-specifieke controle/veiligheid in VRET en het verschil in therapeutische begeleiding tussen condities. Die laatste reflectie is inhoudelijk relevant en studie-specifiek, en laat zien dat de student kritisch nadenkt over alternatieve verklaringen en designimplicaties. Ook worden implicaties voor vervolgonderzoek concreet gemaakt met een passend vier-conditiesdesign. Er zijn wel enkele zwakkere punten: sommige interpretaties zijn speculatief en sterker geformuleerd dan de data toelaten, en de passage waarin het verschil in begeleiding eerst als mogelijke confound wordt genoemd maar daarna niet als confound wordt beschouwd, blijft conceptueel wat wankel. Verder had de koppeling aan de in de introductie genoemde theorie nog systematischer gekund. Toch is de discussie coherent, relevant, behoorlijk volledig en overtuigend voor dit niveau.
lang_style_feedback: De tekst is over het algemeen goed leesbaar en wetenschappelijk van toon, met een duidelijke sectie-indeling en meestal logische alinea-opbouw. De argumentatieve lijn is meestal te volgen en de formuleringen zijn vaak passend voor een academisch paper op bachelor-2 niveau. In APA/verwijzingen zitten enkele onnauwkeurigheden en inconsistenties, bijvoorbeeld in jaartallen van bronnen, bronvermeldingen die niet helemaal aansluiten op de lopende tekst, en referentielijstformattering die niet overal consequent is. De stijl is dus voldoende tot degelijk, maar niet strak genoeg voor een hogere beoordeling.

intro_feedback: De introductie bevat een duidelijke maatschappelijke relevantie, definieert de kernbegrippen goed en bouwt redelijk logisch toe naar de onderzoeksvraag en hypothesen. Sterk is dat de tekst uitlegt waarom sociale angststoornis bij adolescenten belangrijk is, waarom exposure relevant is, en waarom VRET potentieel aantrekkelijk is voor deze doelgroep. Ook is er sprake van enige theoretische onderbouwing, met name via het cognitief-gedragsmatige model van vermijding en zelfgerichte aandacht. De onderzoeksvraag en hypothesen zijn aan het einde duidelijk geformuleerd. Wel blijft de literatuurverwerking deels beschrijvend in plaats van echt synthetiserend. (2016) wordt onjuist gebruikt als inhoudelijke effectstudie terwijl dit in de referentielijst een meta-analyse is, en Bouchard et al. wordt in de tekst als 2017 genoemd maar in de literatuurlijst als 2016 opgenomen. methods_feedback: De methode beschrijft een coherent onderzoeksdesign dat aansluit bij de onderzoeksvraag: drie condities, random toewijzing, pre-postmeting en een passende uitkomstmaat. De deelnemerssectie bevat relevante informatie zoals leeftijd, geslacht, inclusie- en exclusiecriteria. De beschrijving van de interventies is te globaal: vooral voor VRET blijft onduidelijk welke virtuele sociale situaties zijn gebruikt, hoe exposure werd opgebouwd, wat exact gestandaardiseerd was tussen VRET en IVET, en hoe therapeuten handelden. Ook ontbreekt een aparte analysesectie, terwijl die volgens de richtlijnen wel verwacht mag worden. Daarnaast introduceert de IVET-procedure een verschil in begeleiding dat methodologisch relevant is, maar dit wordt pas in de discussie echt kritisch uitgewerkt.
